questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Inferring the Start Time
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a first detected transcript tells you about the start of transcription
questions.stem: In the revision group, Aoife says that a gene's transcript was first detected 4 minutes after the polymerase was added. Explain what this tells the group about when transcription started.

answer.exemplar: The transcript can only be detected once enough of it has accumulated to be measured, so the first detected signal marks the earliest possible moment that transcription had begun, not the moment it actually started. The true start was earlier, and the difference of four minutes reflects the delay in building a detectable amount of RNA plus the time taken for the signal to be measured. Later sampling points would then be offset by the same amount.

questions.explanation: A detected transcript proves only that transcription had already begun, so 4 minutes is the latest possible start, and the real start was earlier. Detecting a product cannot fix the moment of its origin.
questions.hint: Detection lags behind production.

answer.exemplar: Use a system in which a specific messenger RNA can be destroyed on demand, so that any protein still made must come from a transcript made before the switch. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Messenger RNA Decay: Reading a Half-Life
questions.learningObjective: Explain how transcript half-life affects how quickly protein levels change
questions.stem: In the revision group, Lena explains why a messenger RNA with a short half-life controls how quickly a protein can change. Explain her reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A messenger RNA molecule is used for translation a number of times before it is broken down, and the protein it makes may then be degraded at its own rate, which is usually slower. A transcript with a short half-life therefore stops supplying new protein soon after its production is switched off, so the protein level falls quickly and the cell can respond within minutes. A long-lived transcript keeps supplying protein even after the signal stops, so the response is slower and lasts longer.

questions.explanation: A short-lived transcript stops being translated soon after production stops, so the protein level changes quickly, whereas a long-lived transcript keeps the signal going. The decay of the protein also sets how long the change lasts.
questions.hint: Think about how long the message keeps working.

questions.stem: The revision group must show that unwinding happens before new strands are made. Design a way to order the two events.

answer.exemplar: Use a reaction in which the enzyme that opens the duplex is inhibited, and measure the amount of new strand made, alongside a matched reaction with no inhibitor and a reaction given an inactive inhibitor. If the inhibited reaction makes no new strand while the other two behave the same, unwinding must come first, because preventing it stops all synthesis. Adding the inhibitor after synthesis has begun and seeing synthesis continue would confirm the order from the other direction.

questions.explanation: Blocking an early step and seeing synthesis stop, while the controls behave the same, shows the blocked step comes first. Blocking it after synthesis has started and seeing synthesis continue confirms the order.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the link between coding sequence length and protein length
questions.stem: In the revision group, Dan explains how a protein of 180 amino acids relates to the coding sequence of its gene. Explain the relationship.

answer.exemplar: Each amino acid is specified by a codon of three nucleotides, so a protein of 180 amino acids is encoded by 180 times 3, which is 540 nucleotides, and a stop codon of a further three nucleotides marks the end of the coding sequence. A mutation that changes one nucleotide inside that region can alter a single amino acid, and a change that adds a stop codon early can shorten the protein, which is why the length of the coding sequence predicts the length of the product.

questions.explanation: Three nucleotides per amino acid means 180 amino acids need 540 nucleotides, and the stop signal adds a further triplet. Coding length and protein length are therefore fixed in a predictable ratio.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Lagging Strand: Counting Primers
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the lagging strand needs more primers than the leading strand
questions.stem: In the revision group, Ravi explains why the number of primers needed to copy a lagging strand is larger than the number needed for the leading strand. Explain.

answer.exemplar: The leading strand is copied continuously from a single starting point, so one primer is enough for the whole strand. The lagging strand is copied in short Okazaki fragments, each of which has to be started separately because the polymerase cannot begin in the middle of a template without its own primer. The number of primers therefore equals the number of fragments, which is the strand length divided by the fragment length, and is much greater than one.

questions.explanation: One primer starts the continuously copied leading strand, whereas the lagging strand needs a primer for every Okazaki fragment, so its primer count equals the fragment count and is far greater than one.
questions.hint: Continuous copying versus many short fragments.

questions.topic: Transcription: Inferring the Start Time
questions.learningObjective: Design a method for estimating the true start of transcription
questions.stem: To find when transcription actually started rather than when the transcript was first detected, the group must design a method.

answer.exemplar: Collect a series of samples at closely spaced intervals after the polymerase is added and measure the amount of transcript in each, then plot the readings against time. A straight line that meets the zero line at a time earlier than the first sample shows when production began, because the first detection was delayed by the need to accumulate a measurable amount. Extending the line back is more reliable than trusting the first positive sample alone, and an uninduced control shows the background level.

questions.explanation: Sampling at short intervals and extrapolating the linear rise back to zero estimates the true start, since the first positive sample is always late. An uninduced control establishes the background against which the rise is judged.
questions.hint: Sample often and extrapolate backwards.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a very low error rate still matters over a whole genome
questions.stem: In the revision group, Ingrid explains why a very low per nucleotide copying error rate still adds up over a whole genome. Explain her reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The error rate is per nucleotide, so the expected number of errors in a molecule is the genome length multiplied by that rate, and a large genome has a very large total of nucleotides. Even a rate of one in a billion gives several errors per copy of a genome of billions of base pairs, and every one of those errors is inherited in the daughter cell if it is not repaired. This is why accuracy depends on both proofreading and repair after copying, not on matching alone.

questions.explanation: Errors accumulate in proportion to the number of nucleotides copied, so a billion-base genome carries several errors per copy even at a tiny rate. Repair after copying matters for the same reason.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a single base change can alter the length of a protein
questions.stem: Lena explains to the revision group why a single base change in a coding sequence can produce a protein of a different length. Explain.

answer.exemplar: A codon that specifies an amino acid can be changed by a single base substitution into one of the three stop codons, and the ribosome then stops there, so the chain is cut short and a truncated protein is made. In the other direction, a base change can convert a stop codon into one that specifies an amino acid, and translation continues into what was previously untranslated sequence, giving a longer protein. This is why a single nucleotide substitution can change the length of a product and not just one of its building blocks.

questions.explanation: A substitution can create or destroy a stop codon, so the ribosome stops earlier or later and the protein changes length. Saying such a change always affects only one amino acid misses the early stop case.

answer.exemplar: The promoter is a binding site rather than a transcribed stretch. answer.exemplar: Sequence a copy of the genome and compare the sequence with a high quality reference of the same region, and repeat the sequencing on independently copied samples so that differences are not simply sequencing mistakes. questions.topic: Gene Expression: From DNA to a Working Protein
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one genome gives rise to many different proteins
questions.stem: In the revision group, Aoife explains why a cell may make many different proteins from the same genome. Explain her reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Different genes are switched on and off at different times and in different cells, and each gene that is on is transcribed into its own messenger RNA and translated into its own protein, so the protein output of a cell depends on its pattern of gene expression rather than on the genome alone. questions.topic: DNA Replication: Sequencing the Events at a Fork
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the events at a replication fork occur in a fixed order
questions.stem: Lena explains to the group how the events at a replication fork are ordered so that copying works. Explain her reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The order follows from what each step needs from the one before it. The duplex is opened first, because paired bases inside a stable double helix are not available to be read. Templates are then exposed and held apart, so the polymerase can read them and add complementary nucleotides to a primer, forming the new strands. Only after the strand is largely complete are the RNA primers removed, the gaps filled and the nicks sealed, which is the final tidy-up of the lagging strand.

questions.explanation: Each step depends on the one before: unwinding exposes templates, copying needs exposed templates and a primer, and the cleanup of primers and nicks comes last. Rearranging the steps would leave a step without what it needs.
questions.hint: Ask what each step needs from the last.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Messenger RNA Decay: Reading a Half-Life
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the transcript remaining after a further half-life
questions.stem: Tonight's revision shows a transcript at 30 percent of its starting amount after two half-lives. What percentage remains after a third half-life?
questions.explanation: Each half-life halves what is left, so 30 divided by 2 is 15 percent after a third half-life. An answer of 10 would halve the 30 twice more, and 60 would double the amount instead of halving it.
questions.hint: Halve the remaining percentage.
